title: A Triumph of Surgery
summary: This humorous story by James Herriot shows how blind love can harm as much as illness. Mrs Pumphrey, a rich lady, adores her small dog Tricki and expresses her affection by feeding him malt, cod liver oil, Horlicks, cream cakes and chocolates between meals while giving him no exercise at all. Tricki becomes hugely fat, listless and dull, with rheumy eyes, and soon suffers bouts of vomiting. The narrator, a wise veterinary surgeon, had already warned that only dieting and exercise could save the dog, but the fond lady could not refuse him anything. When she panics, the vet takes Tricki to his surgery, gives him no food for two days and only plenty of water, and then lets him run and play with the other dogs. Tempted by their food and games, Tricki eats, romps and rapidly becomes lithe and energetic. The eggs, wine and brandy his mistress keeps sending are cheerfully consumed by the doctor and his partners. When the healthy Tricki leaps into her car, Mrs Pumphrey gratefully exclaims that it is a triumph of surgery, unaware that fasting, water and common sense, not surgery, have cured him.

Cause of Tricki's illness: overfeeding and lack of exercise
The vet's simple cure: fasting, water and exercise
Irony and humour in the title A Triumph of Surgery
Character sketch of Mrs Pumphrey as a rich but foolish mistress
Mr Herriot as a wise, tactful and kind veterinary surgeon

sections.heading: About the Author
sections.para: James Herriot is the pen name of James Alfred Wight, an English veterinary surgeon who became one of the best loved writers of animal stories. Born in 1916, he grew up in Glasgow and spent his working life as a country vet in the Yorkshire Dales, treating farm animals and household pets of every kind. His celebrated books, such as All Creatures Great and Small and All Things Bright and Beautiful, grew directly out of the real animals and owners he met in daily practice. His style is simple, warm and conversational, marked by gentle humour, keen observation and deep sympathy for animals and their owners. He believed that true episodes from a doctor's life make better reading than invented drama, which is why his tales feel so authentic. In A Triumph of Surgery he converts a routine case of an overfed pet into a comic story that quietly teaches that sensible care is better than blind affection.
points: James Herriot was the pen name of James Alfred Wight, an English veterinary surgeon born in 1916 who became famous for his animal stories.
He grew up in Glasgow and practised as a country vet in Yorkshire, drawing all his material from the animals and farmers he actually treated.
His famous books include All Creatures Great and Small and All Things Bright and Beautiful, records of the warm and funny episodes of a vet's life.
His writing is simple, conversational and full of gentle humour, keen observation of animal behaviour and sympathy for owners as well as pets.
He believed real professional experiences make better stories than invented plots, which gives his tales their authentic ring.
In A Triumph of Surgery he turns a genuine case of an overfed pet into comedy with a moral about sensible care.

keyTerms.meaning: A doctor trained to treat the diseases of animals; the author's profession and the narrator's role in the story.
A name used by a writer instead of his real one; James Alfred Wight wrote as James Herriot.
A short, interesting tale based on real personal experience, the form of this story.
Comedy arising from close watching of real people and animals, the chief flavour of Herriot's writing.
The story is told in the I voice by the vet himself, which brings the reader inside the surgery.

sections.trick: VET stands for Very Entertaining Tale teller: James Herriot was a Yorkshire vet who turned his daily cases into classic comic stories.
sections.examPointer: A 2 marker may ask why Herriot's animal stories feel so real; always mention that he was a practising veterinary surgeon writing from firsthand experience, and that the narrator of this story is a vet.

sections.heading: Background and Setting
sections.para: The story grows out of the professional life of a Yorkshire veterinary surgeon of the early twentieth century. Mrs Pumphrey, a rich lady of the neighbourhood, keeps a small dog, Tricki, and treats him like a pampered human child instead of an animal. Dogs are natural runners and players, and the conflict of the story arises because Tricki is denied the very things a dog needs most, namely plain food and free play. The vet's surgery, with its kennels, its ordinary canine patients and its simple food, forms a deliberate contrast with the cushions, coats and delicacies of Mrs Pumphrey's house. In fashionable households of that age, love for pets was often measured by rich meals, soft beds and medical fuss, and this is precisely the folly the story satirises. The setting allows the author to place an animal doctor between a foolishly fond owner and a suffering animal, which is the classic triangle of all his tales.
points: The story is set in the world of a country vet in Yorkshire, drawn from James Herriot's own practice.
Mrs Pumphrey is a wealthy lady who treats her pet dog Tricki like a spoilt human child rather than an animal.
The disease in the story is not medical but social: fashionable love expressed through rich food and soft living.
The vet's surgery, full of normal, energetic dogs, is the opposite world of plain food and natural habits.
The humour depends on this contrast between luxury at home and simplicity at the surgery.
The setting creates the classic triangle of Herriot's stories: a wise vet between a fond owner and a suffering animal.

keyTerms.meaning: Indulging someone so excessively that his real needs are neglected; Mrs Pumphrey's way of loving Tricki.
In British usage, a doctor's clinic; Tricki is taken to the vet's surgery, not to an operating theatre.
Rich, tasty foods like cream cakes and chocolates, useless and harmful for a dog.
The gradual recovery of health after illness, achieved by Tricki through rest, plain food and play.
A small shelter for a dog, the plain healthy home at the surgery compared with Tricki's luxurious cushions.

sections.trick: Contrast card: the HOME of luxury made Tricki ILL, the CLINIC of plainness made him WELL.
sections.examPointer: Questions may ask where Tricki was taken and why; remember that the surgery means the vet's clinic, and that removing the dog from his mistress's pampering was itself half the cure.

sections.heading: Plot Overview
sections.para: Tricki, the small pet dog of the rich Mrs Pumphrey, is stuffed between meals with malt, cod liver oil, Horlicks, cream cakes and chocolates and is given no exercise, so that he becomes hugely fat and listless, with rheumy eyes and a lolling tongue, like a bloated sausage. When he begins to have bouts of vomiting, his mistress rings up the vet in panic. The vet had already warned that the only remedy was to cut down food, stop sweets and make the dog exercise, so he now decides to hospitalise Tricki at his surgery, knowing that the real disease is over pampering. Mrs Pumphrey almost swoons as the dog is carried off, and then telephones daily and sends eggs, wine and brandy for the patient. At the surgery Tricki gets no food for two days and only plenty of water, and no medicine at all. Tempted by the sight and smell of the other dogs' food and drawn into their games, he eats, runs, rolls and romps, and soon becomes lithe and energetic. When he leaps joyfully into her car, Mrs Pumphrey exclaims that it is a triumph of surgery.
points: Tricki is overfed between meals with malt, cod liver oil, Horlicks, cream cakes and chocolates and is given no exercise.
He becomes hugely fat and listless, with rheumy eyes and a lolling tongue, and finally has bouts of vomiting.
The vet had clearly advised cutting down food, forbidding sweets and giving exercise, but the fond lady could not follow it.
On her panic telephone call the vet decides to hospitalise Tricki at once, and Mrs Pumphrey almost swoons as the dog is carried away.
The strict treatment is no food for two days and plenty of water, with no medicine of any kind.
The turning point comes when hungry Tricki watches the other dogs being fed and is drawn into their games.
He recovers rapidly, becoming lithe and hard muscled, while the eggs, wine and brandy sent for him are enjoyed by the vet and his partners.
At the reunion Mrs Pumphrey gratefully exclaims that it is a triumph of surgery, unaware that fasting and play have done the work.

keyTerms.meaning: Dull and without energy; the overfed Tricki lies about listlessly.
Watery and discharging, used of the eyes of the sick dog.
Swollen with food and fat; Tricki is compared to a bloated sausage.
Repeated attacks of vomiting that frighten Mrs Pumphrey into calling the vet.
Flexible and gracefully slim, the condition Tricki regains after play and plain diet.

sections.trick: Fat, Call, Fast, Play, Hooray: overfed dog, panic call, two day fast, games with dogs, joyride home.
sections.examPointer: The most repeated 3 to 4 marker asks what made Tricki ill and how he was cured; always mention overfeeding, no exercise, the two day fast, plenty of water and exercise with the other dogs.

sections.heading: Character Sketch: Mrs Pumphrey
sections.para: Mrs Pumphrey is a picture of warm hearted but blind love. Rich and generous, she cannot refuse Tricki anything: she feeds him between meals, gives him coats, cushions and a whole wardrobe, and worries herself sick at the least sign of illness. Her love is genuine, for she nearly faints when the dog is taken away, telephones the surgery daily, and sends eggs, wine and brandy for the patient; yet it is also foolish, because she cannot see that her own indulgence is the cause of his sickness, and she ignores the vet's plain advice about diet and exercise. She is emotional and dramatic, treating a case of overeating like a mortal illness. At the same time she is grateful and warm, thanking the vet extravagantly when Tricki recovers and joyfully crediting a surgery that never happened. Through her the author satirises rich owners who substitute luxuries for an understanding of an animal's real needs, and shows that affection without sense can be dangerous.
points: Mrs Pumphrey is rich, kind hearted and lavish, and treats her pet like a spoilt princeling.
She is blind in her love: she feeds Tricki between meals and gives him coats, cushions and a whole wardrobe.
She is over anxious: the least sign of illness sends her rushing to the telephone, and she nearly swoons when Tricki is taken away.
She is generous to a fault, sending eggs, wine and brandy for the patient and expecting everyone to share her worry.
She lacks common sense: she cannot accept that indulgence, not disease, has made Tricki ill, and she ignores the vet's advice.
She is grateful and emotional, thanking the vet extravagantly and calling the recovery a triumph of surgery.
Through her the author satirises rich owners who express love through luxuries instead of understanding natural needs.

keyTerms.meaning: Showing extreme, foolish fondness; Mrs Pumphrey is a doting mistress.
Spending lavishly and beyond need, like her gifts of delicacies and clothing for a dog.
Full of worry; she panics at every small sign of Tricki's discomfort.
Foolishness; her loving but senseless pampering nearly kills the dog.
Thankfulness, which she shows warmly to the vet at the happy ending.

sections.trick: Mrs Pumphrey equals the three P's: POUNDS, PAMPERING and PANIC, backed by a soft heart and a blind eye.
sections.examPointer: Whether Mrs Pumphrey was a good mistress is a favourite 4 to 5 marker; write a balanced sketch contrasting her genuine love and generosity with her foolish indulgence, supporting each side with an instance.

sections.heading: Character Sketch: Mr Herriot and Tricki
sections.para: The narrator, Mr Herriot, is a wise, practical and compassionate veterinary surgeon who understands animals better than their owners do. He is firm yet tactful: instead of lecturing Mrs Pumphrey, he quietly takes Tricki to his surgery and applies a strict but kind cure, knowing that argument would be useless. He treats causes and not merely symptoms, judging at once that overfeeding, not disease, has made the dog ill. He is also quietly humorous and human, for he lets his partners enjoy the useless eggs, wine and brandy without guilt, since he knows they can do Tricki no good. Tricki, the patient, is a lovable, greedy little dog who mirrors his mistress: stuffed with delicacies he becomes a bloated, whining invalid, but once hunger and play return, his natural dogginess revives and he romps with the pack like any healthy animal. Together the wise doctor and the recovered dog prove the story's point that sensible treatment and natural living beat luxuries and medicines.
points: Mr Herriot is a sensible, kind and firm veterinary surgeon with an accurate understanding of animals.
He is tactful: he does not argue with Mrs Pumphrey but acts quietly, taking Tricki to the surgery for a strict cure.
He diagnoses the true cause of the illness, overfeeding without exercise, and treats the cause rather than the symptoms.
He is humorous and unpretentious, cheerfully consuming the eggs, wine and brandy that were useless to the patient.
Tricki is a lovable, greedy dog who mirrors his mistress and becomes an invalid on rich food and cushions.
Deprived of food Tricki first sulks mournfully on his rug, but the sight of the other dogs eating awakens his appetite and spirit.
The recovery of Tricki vindicates the vet's common sense approach of fasting, water and exercise.

keyTerms.meaning: Skill in handling people without offending them, shown by the vet towards Mrs Pumphrey.
Identifying the true nature of an illness; the vet diagnoses over pampering, not disease.
Practical good judgement, the real medicine used in the story.
Sympathetic concern for suffering, which the vet shows for the dog while staying firm.
Natural behaviour; Tricki's inborn love of food and play returns and heals him.

sections.trick: Herriot equals HEAD plus HEART: head for correct diagnosis, heart for animals; Tricki equals TURNAROUND, from sofa invalid to park champion.
sections.examPointer: A long answer may ask for the character of the vet; stress his correct diagnosis, firmness, tact and common sense treatment, and add that he is humorous rather than preachy.

sections.heading: Themes and Message
sections.para: The chief theme of the story is that excess of everything is bad. Overfeeding and lack of exercise, though given with love, nearly kill Tricki, and discipline, not drugs, cures him. Blind love is contrasted with intelligent love: real affection seeks the welfare of the loved one and sometimes must say no, exactly as a wise parent refuses a child's demands. The story gently satirises the rich, who express affection through luxuries while ignoring natural needs, and it upholds the professional duty of a doctor who treats the patient honestly rather than pleasing the family. It also shows that animals are happiest in their natural state of activity and plain food, not as invalids on sofas with coats and tonics. Behind the comedy lies a serious lesson on self control that applies equally to pets, children and human habits, making the story both funny and wise.
points: Excess of everything is bad: overfeeding and no exercise, however lovingly given, made Tricki seriously ill.
Blind love harms; intelligent love seeks the welfare of the loved one and sometimes must refuse.
Discipline and simple living cure better than medicines: fasting, water and play restore what tonics and delicacies ruined.
The story satirises the rich who substitute luxuries for understanding of an animal's real needs.
Professional duty means honest treatment: the vet serves the patient rather than the owner's feelings.
Animals thrive on natural diet and free activity, not on cushions, coats and constant feeding.

keyTerms.meaning: An outcome opposite to what is expected; calling fasting and exercise a triumph of surgery is deeply ironic.
Gentle ridicule of human follies, here the folly of pampering owners.
Regular control over food and habits, the real medicine that cured Tricki.
Yielding to every wish of a person or animal, which nearly killed Tricki.
Avoidance of excess, the message of the story in matters of food and comfort.

sections.trick: LOVE plus LUXURY equals ILLNESS; LOVE plus LIMITS equals HEALTH.
sections.examPointer: The irony of the title is a classic 2 to 3 marker; explain that no surgery took place and that the real triumph was that of common sense over pampering.

sections.heading: Humour, Irony and the Title
sections.para: The humour of the story is gentle and situational, arising from character rather than from jokes. We smile at the spectacle of a fat dog carried in like an important person, at a grown lady weeping over a simple case of overeating, and at the doctor and his partners cheerfully consuming the eggs, wine and brandy meant for the patient. The comic contrast lies between the solemn fuss at Mrs Pumphrey's end and the plain horse sense at the surgery. The deepest joke is the irony of the title: no operation, no medicine and no surgery of any kind take place, yet the cure is hailed as a triumph of surgery. The title flatters the ignorance of the loving owner and celebrates, unknown to her, the victory of fasting, water and exercise. Thus the story is comedy with a conscience: it makes readers laugh while quietly teaching them how to care for those they love.
points: The humour is situational and gentle, growing naturally out of character and event.
We laugh at the fat dog carried like an invalid dignitary and at the lady's dramatic despair over overeating.
The comic contrast is between luxurious fuss at home and plain sense at the surgery.
The staff enjoying the patient's eggs, wine and brandy is a running comic thread.
The title is ironic: a triumph of surgery is declared although no surgery was ever performed.
The real triumph belongs to fasting, water, exercise and common sense, which the mistress never learns.

keyTerms.meaning: Laughter arising from circumstances and situations rather than from wordplay.
A title whose real meaning is the opposite of its surface claim, as here.
A fall from grand expectation to plain reality, as when surgery turns out to be fasting.
Mild ridicule that corrects folly without bitterness.
A repeated comic element, here the daily parcels of eggs, wine and brandy.

sections.trick: No knife, no pill, no cut, yet the title says surgery: Tricki was cured by the treatment of the absent kind, food absent and pampering absent.
sections.examPointer: When asked to justify the title, first state what surgery means, then prove that no surgery happened, and finally name the real cure; this three step answer fetches full marks.

sections.heading: Important Incidents and Value Points
sections.para: Memorable incidents crowd the story. First comes the panic telephone call in which Mrs Pumphrey reports bouts of vomiting and total listlessness, and the vet orders hospitalisation. Then the near swoon: the fond lady almost faints as Tricki is carried off whining mournfully in the vet's car. The strict regime follows: for two days the patient gets no food, only plenty of water, and no medicine whatsoever. The turning point arrives when hungry Tricki watches the other dogs being fed, and the smell and sight of plain food reawaken his appetite. Soon he chases, rolls and romps with the pack, and the fat melts away as his spirits rise. Meanwhile eggs for breakfast, wine for lunch and brandy at night arrive daily and are greatly appreciated by the vet and his partners. Finally a quivering, delighted Tricki flings himself into his mistress's car, and she drives off announcing a triumph of surgery. The value points are clear: too much love can kill, honest professional advice must be heeded, and natural diet and exercise are the best medicine.
points: The panic telephone call: Mrs Pumphrey reports vomiting and listlessness and the vet orders hospitalisation.
The near swoon: the fond lady almost faints as Tricki is carried away from her.
The strict regime: two days of fasting with nothing but water and no medicine at all.
The turning point: Tricki watches the other dogs being fed and his appetite and spirit revive.
The games: Tricki runs, rolls and romps with the pack and rapidly sheds his fatness.
The comic luxury: eggs, wine and brandy arrive daily for the patient and are consumed by the staff.
The reunion: a delighted Tricki leaps into the car and Mrs Pumphrey proclaims a triumph of surgery.
Value points: excess love harms, honest advice must be followed, and natural living is the best medicine.

keyTerms.meaning: Keeping a patient under treatment in a clinic; here it means removing Tricki from pampering.
Going without food for a period, the simple treatment the overfed dog needed.
A planned course of diet and activity, enforced strictly at the surgery.
The joyful coming together of Tricki and Mrs Pumphrey at the end.
The moral or lesson a story teaches, the part CBSE answers must always add.

sections.trick: Eight beads on a string: FAT DOG, PANIC CALL, CAR RIDE, TWO DAY FAST, FOOD SIGHT, WILD GAMES, FREE WINES, CAR JUMP.
sections.examPointer: Long answers often ask you to describe the treatment at the surgery or Tricki's daily routine there; keep the fasting, the water, the watching of other dogs and the games as your four core points.

boardQuestions.question: What advice of the veterinary surgeon did Mrs Pumphrey fail to follow, and with what result?
boardQuestions.answer: The vet had advised Mrs Pumphrey to cut down Tricki's food, take away the sweets and titbits between meals, and make the dog take regular exercise. The fond lady could not bear to see Tricki hungry or tired, so she went on feeding him cream cakes, chocolates, malt, cod liver oil and Horlicks and let him lie on his cushions. As a result Tricki became hugely fat and listless, developed rheumy eyes and finally began to have bouts of vomiting, which frightened his mistress into calling the vet again.

boardQuestions.question: Why did the vet decide to take Tricki away to his surgery? What did he say to satisfy Mrs Pumphrey?
boardQuestions.answer: 1) The vet knew at once that there was nothing really wrong with Tricki's body; the dog was sick because of overfeeding and lack of exercise. 2) He also knew that Mrs Pumphrey would never agree to diet her darling, and would go on pampering him at home, so the only way to control the food was to take the dog to his surgery. 3) He therefore told her gravely that Tricki must be hospitalised immediately without delay, and the shocked lady, though she almost swooned at parting, consented. 4) Thus the removal itself was the first half of the treatment, for away from her tender care the dog could be kept hungry and active as his nature demanded.

boardQuestions.question: Why did Mrs Pumphrey send eggs, wine and brandy to the surgery? What do these parcels reveal about her?
boardQuestions.answer: 1) Mrs Pumphrey believed that her darling was gravely ill in hospital and needed building up, so she sent eggs to be given at breakfast, wine at lunch and brandy at night. 2) The parcels reveal her genuine love, her wealth and her habit of expressing affection through luxuries, since she imagined that delicacies could cure where dieting was actually at work. 3) They also reveal her folly and her ignorance of a dog's needs, for Tricki wanted plain food and exercise, not rich drinks. 4) The comic result is that the vet and his partners consumed the whole supply themselves, and the story gently laughs at loving owners who mistake luxury for care.

boardQuestions.question: Describe the treatment given to Tricki at the surgery. How did it bring about his complete recovery?
boardQuestions.answer: 1) When Tricki reached the surgery, the veterinary surgeon made his diagnosis at once: the dog had no organic disease, and his sickness was the direct result of overfeeding and lack of exercise. 2) He therefore decided that no medicine and no operation were required; what Tricki needed was discipline and a return to natural ways. 3) For the first two days the patient was given no food at all, only plenty of water, so that his overloaded system could rest; Tricki lay on his rug, mournful and weak, whining at nothing, but the vet stood firm and did not yield to his pleading eyes. 4) On the following days the starving dog's eyes brightened; when the other dogs were fed, Tricki hovered near them, sniffed at their bowls and, tempted by the smell and sight of plain food, began to eat. 5) He was then allowed to join the pack; he rolled on the grass, chased his new companions and plunged into their games with growing delight. 6) Day by day his fat melted away; he became lithe, hard muscled and full of bounce, with bright eyes and a ready bark. 7) Meanwhile the eggs, wine and brandy sent by his mistress were quietly enjoyed by the vet and his partners, for the dog needed none of them. 8) Thus the cure was a triumph not of surgery but of common sense, and Tricki bounded back to his owner in perfect health.

boardQuestions.question: Draw a character sketch of Mrs Pumphrey, supporting your answer with instances from the story.
boardQuestions.answer: 1) Mrs Pumphrey is a rich, warm hearted and generous lady who loves her little dog Tricki more than anything in the world, but her love is blind and foolish. 2) She treats him like a spoilt child: he gets cream cakes and chocolates between meals, malt, cod liver oil and Horlicks, coats and cushions and a whole wardrobe, while exercise is thought unnecessary for a gentleman of comfort. 3) She is emotional and over anxious; when Tricki becomes listless and starts vomiting she rings up the vet in panic, and she nearly swoons when the dog is carried off to the surgery. 4) Her love continues at a distance: she telephones every day, asks anxiously after him, and sends eggs, wine and brandy to build up his strength, never realising that luxuries are the disease and not the cure. 5) She cannot follow plain advice, because refusing Tricki anything is beyond her nature, and this weakness nearly kills the dog she adores. 6) At the same time she is grateful and warm hearted; when Tricki bounds into her car, cured and joyful, she thanks the vet and exclaims happily that it is a triumph of surgery. 7) Thus she is a lovable fool, and through her the author satirises rich owners who mistake indulgence for affection, showing that true love must be wise enough to discipline.

boardQuestions.question: Read the extract: Mrs Pumphrey rang up in a trembling voice to say that Tricki had bouts of vomiting, lay listless and would touch nothing. The vet knew at once that there was nothing seriously wrong with the dog's body, but he also knew that the loving lady would never accept the truth. He said that Tricki must be hospitalised immediately, and Mrs Pumphrey almost swooned as the little dog was carried away. (a) What, according to the vet, was the real cause of Tricki's illness? (b) Why did he take Tricki to his surgery instead of treating him at home? (c) What does the episode show about the relationship between love and discipline?
boardQuestions.answer: (a) The vet knew that Tricki was not suffering from any disease of the body; his listlessness and vomiting were caused by overfeeding on rich food and sweets and by the complete absence of exercise. (b) Had he treated Tricki at home, Mrs Pumphrey would have continued to feed and cosset him, defeating every instruction; by taking the dog to his surgery the vet could control the diet strictly, keep the mistress's indulgence out of reach, and enforce fasting and later exercise with the other dogs. (c) The episode shows that love without discipline harms the loved one: true affection means doing what is good rather than what is pleasing. It was separation, plain water and play, not pampering, that restored Tricki, so wise love must sometimes be firm, even at the cost of brief pain.

boardQuestions.question: Do you think Mrs Pumphrey really loved Tricki? What lesson does the story teach about the right way to love and care, whether for pets or for children?
boardQuestions.answer: 1) Mrs Pumphrey truly loved Tricki; her worry, her daily telephone calls and the costly parcels she sent prove that her affection was real, not pretended. 2) Yet her love was blind, because she never asked what a dog actually needs; she gave him what pleased herself, and her indulgence of rich food and soft living nearly killed him. 3) The story teaches that genuine care must be guided by knowledge and discipline: we should give the loved one what is good for him, not what momentarily pleases him, and we must have the strength to say no. 4) The same lesson applies to parents who pamper children with luxuries and shield them from all effort, for such love weakens rather than strengthens. 5) The vet's success shows that firm, sensible kindness, though it may look harsh for a moment, is the highest form of love.

boardQuestions.question: The story A Triumph of Surgery is a gentle satire on the rich and their blind affection. Discuss with instances from the text.
boardQuestions.answer: 1) Satire means the ridicule of human follies in order to correct them, and Herriot's target here is the fashionable rich who love their pets foolishly. 2) Mrs Pumphrey measures love in luxuries: Tricki has coats for cold days and raincoats for wet ones, a whole wardrobe, bowls for different meals, a day bed, a night bed and favourite cushions, and between meals a stream of malt, cod liver oil, Horlicks, cream cakes and chocolates. 3) The satire sharpens when she treats a simple case of overeating as a mortal illness, ringing the vet in panic, swooning at separation and telephoning daily as if the dog were on his deathbed. 4) The climax of the comedy is the daily parade of eggs, wine and brandy sent to build up a patient who is actually being starved back to health, and which the vet and his partners consume with relish. 5) The final irony completes the satire: the lady gratefully credits a triumph of surgery where there was no surgery at all, only fasting and play. 6) Thus the story laughs at the folly of confusing indulgence with care, and quietly instructs its readers that animals need natural food, freedom and exercise rather than rich food and fuss.
